This overview is created with [Quarto](https://quarto.org) and uses the [R](https://www.r-project.org/) programming language for statistics and plotting
(see [source file](quantitative-analysis-examples.qmd)).
The analyses and plots shown here are based on [real-world data](data/).

```{r}
#| label: load-libraries
#| message: false

# Load necessary libraries
library(tidyverse) # for analyses and plots

# Increase console output width
options("width" = 100)
```

## Obtaining and Preparing the data

Read data from the CSV file.
It is mostly clean already, so we only need to standardize two different `NA` values,
and introduce a new variable `script` to summarize types of programming languages.

```{r}
#| label: load-data
df <- read_csv("data/jccpprtTR.csv", col_types = "ccddiidddf") |>
    mutate(
        # Standardize and order caps column
        caps = caps |> fct_na_level_to_value(extra_levels = c("??", "NA")),
        caps = caps |> fct_relevel(sort(levels(caps))),
        # New boolean variable for convenience
        script = lang %in% c("perl", "python", "rexx", "tcl")
    )

df |> print(n = 5)
```

## Exploring the Data

We use descriptive statistics and simple plots to take a first look at our data.

### Average Work Hours per Programming Language

```{r}
#| label: calc-avg-whours
df |>
    summarize(avg_whours = mean(whours), .by = lang)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-java-whours
#| fig-cap: Work time spent on Java programs
#| warning: false
df |>
    filter(lang == "Java") |>
    arrange(whours) |>
    mutate(no = row_number()) |>

    # Bar chart
    ggplot(aes(x = no, y = whours)) +
    geom_col(fill = "orange") +

    # Add horizontal line at mean value
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(whours))) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 1, y = mean(whours)), label = "Mean", check_overlap = TRUE, vjust = -1) +

    # Optics
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_blank()
    )
```

### Visualizing One Variable (Nominal or Ordinal)

Nominal and ordinal variable are best displayed as bar charts.

Avoid pie charts, because two segments of similar size cannot be distinguished as easily as two bars of similar size.

Use qualitative color scales for nominal scales and sequential or diverging for ordinal variables.


```{r} 
#| label: fig-nominal-bar-chart
#| fig-cap: Bar charts work even for nominal variables, because we only need to count.

df |>
    count(lang) |>

    # Bar chart
    ggplot(aes(x = lang, y = n, fill = lang)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity") +

    # Optics
    ylab("count") +
    scale_fill_brewer(type = "qual", palette = "Dark2") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        legend.position = "none",
    )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ordinal-stacked-bar-chart
#| fig-cap: Ordinal variables should be shown in order, possibly even stacked.

df |>
    filter(!is.na(caps)) |>
    count(caps) |>

    # Stacked bar chart
    ggplot(aes(x = 1, y = n, fill = caps)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") +

    # Optics
    coord_flip(xlim = c(0, 2)) +
    ylab("Proportion") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
    scale_fill_brewer(name = "Self-Assessment", type = "div", palette = "RdYlGn", direction = -1) +
    #scale_fill_brewer(name = "Self-Assessment", palette = "RdYlGn", direction = -1) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse=T)) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom",
    )
```

### Visualizing One Variable (Interval or Ratio) with Histograms

```{r}
#| label: fig-histograms
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "Wide bins (here: 50) lead to smoother shapes"
#|   - "Narrow bins (here: 20) lead to jagged shapes"
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 4

histogram <- function(df, binwidth) {
    df |>
        ggplot(aes(x = stmtL)) +
        geom_histogram(fill = "#1e8625ff", color = "white", binwidth = binwidth) +

        # Optics
        coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, NA)) +
        theme_minimal()
}

df |> histogram(50)

df |> histogram(20)
```

### Visualizing One Variable (Interval or Ratio) with Boxplots

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplot
#| fig-cap: A box plot showing the middle 50% (box), median (thick line), min and max without outliers (whiskers), and outliers (separate dots).
#| fig-height: 2

geom_boxplot_custom <- function(...) {
    geom_boxplot(staplewidth = 1, outlier.shape = 1, median.color = "black", ...)
}

df |>
    ggplot(aes(x = stmtL)) +
    geom_boxplot_custom(fill = "#1e8625") +

    # Optics
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(NA, NA), xlim = c(0, NA)) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank()
    )
```

### Visualizing Differences in Data with Boxplots

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplot-compare
#| fig-cap: Box plots allow to quickly compare distributions.
#| fig-height: 4

df |>
    filter(lang %in% c("Java", "C")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = stmtL, y = lang)) +
    geom_boxplot_custom(fill = "#1e8625") +

    # Optics
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(NA, NA), xlim = c(0, NA)) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank()
    )
```

The two languages appear to have the same median, but different dispersion measures.

```{r}
#| label: dispersion-calc
df |>
    filter(lang %in% c("Java", "C")) |>
    summarize(
        smedian = median(stmtL),
        siqr    = IQR(stmtL),
        ssd     = sd(stmtL),
        .by = lang
    )
```

### Visualizing Two Variables: Ratio vs. Ratio with Scatterplots

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatterplot
#| fig-cap: Scatterplots show the relation of two ratio variables (and allow for more variables as well, dot size, shape, color, ...)

df |>
    ggplot(aes(x = whours, y = stmtL)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = script)) +

    # Optics
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, NA), xlim = c(0, NA)) +
    theme_minimal()
```

## Infer from Data

First, you need to decide what you want to test.
Typically, you would test for differences between groups or for correlations between groups.

### Difference Testing

There appears to be a difference in program size between script and non-script languages
(seen in @fig-scatterplot, confirmed in @fig-boxplot-script):

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplot-script
#| fig-cap: Visually, there is a large difference between the size of script and non-script programs.

df |>
    ggplot(aes(x = stmtL, y = script)) +
    geom_boxplot_custom(fill = "#1e8625") +

    # Optics
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(NA, NA), xlim = c(0, NA)) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank()
    )
```

We are testing whether the difference shown in @fig-boxplot-script could be by chance
(i.e., how likely is it to see a at least as big difference in samples of our size assuming there is no difference in the underlying population).
Since the distributions are skewed (non-symmetric) and have a long tail (outliers beyond the boxplot whiskers), we use a non-parametric test (one that does not expect normally-distributed data).

```{r}
#| label: hypothesis-test
#| warning: false
wilcox.test(whours ~ script, data = df)
```

The probability ("p-value") is *way* smaller than 5% -- we accept this as a "statistically significant difference".
But we don't know yet, whether that difference is practically meaningful.

#### Effect Size

```{r}
#| label: effect-size
library(effectsize)

effect_size <- cohens_d(whours ~ script, data = df)
effect_size
```

The effect size `r effect_size$Cohens_d |> round(2)` indicates a large effect (> 0.8).
It means that the two means of the script and non-script languages
are `r effect_size$Cohens_d |> round(2)` standard deviations apart.

### Correlation Testing

```{r}
#| label: fig-regression-analysis
#| fig-cap: "For script languages, there is a moderately strong correlation between the work time and the size of programs."
#| warning: false

r <- with(subset(df, script), cor.test(whours, stmtL, method = "pearson"))

# Scatter plot (of script languages)
subset(df, script) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = whours, y = stmtL)) +
    geom_point(color = "#11c0ccff") +

    # Add regression line (method = "lm" uses the same calculation as Pearson's r under the hood)
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
    # Add r-value
    annotate("text", x = 10, y = 150, 
           label = paste("r =", round(r$estimate, 2), "\np =", format.pval(r$p.value, 2, 0.001, 3)), 
           size = 5, color = "blue") +

    # Optics
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, NA), xlim = c(0, NA)) +
    theme_minimal()
```
